title: The Doctrine of Sovereignty in Modern International Law
excerpt: An examination of how sovereignty has evolved from the Westphalian model to contemporary norms shaped by human rights obligations and multilateral treaties.
content:
The concept of sovereignty remains one of the most contested and evolving doctrines in international legal scholarship. Since the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, the notion of absolute territorial sovereignty has been the bedrock upon which the modern state system was built. However, the latter half of the twentieth century witnessed a dramatic reinterpretation of what sovereignty entails and what obligations accompany it.

The emergence of the United Nations Charter in 1945 introduced a fundamental tension: Article 2(1) affirms the sovereign equality of all member states, while Article 2(7) prohibits interference in matters of domestic jurisdiction. Yet the same Charter empowers the Security Council under Chapter VII to authorize measures that directly impinge upon a state's internal affairs in the name of international peace and security.

This tension came into sharp relief during the NATO intervention in Kosovo in 1999, conducted without explicit Security Council authorization. The subsequent debate gave rise to the 'Responsibility to Protect' (R2P) doctrine, formally adopted at the 2005 World Summit. R2P posits that sovereignty is not merely a right but a responsibility — when a state manifestly fails to protect its population from atrocity crimes, the international community bears a residual duty to act.

Scholars such as Anne-Marie Slaughter and Louis Henkin have argued that this shift represents a 'disaggregation' of sovereignty, where functional competencies rather than absolute territorial control define the modern state. Critics, including China and Russia, contend that R2P provides a pretext for powerful states to intervene in weaker nations under humanitarian guise.

The jurisprudence of the International Court of Justice has navigated these tensions cautiously. In the Nicaragua case (1986), the Court reaffirmed strong non-intervention principles, while in the Genocide Convention cases, it acknowledged that sovereignty cannot shield a state from responsibility for jus cogens violations.

As climate change, pandemics, and transnational terrorism increasingly demand collective responses, the sovereignty doctrine will continue to be reshaped by the practical exigencies of global governance.
author: Lamia Akhter

title: Transboundary Water Rights and the Law of International Watercourses
excerpt: A research analysis of the 1997 UN Watercourses Convention and customary principles governing shared river systems, with focus on the Nile and Mekong basins.
content:
Freshwater scarcity is emerging as one of the defining geopolitical challenges of the 21st century. With over 310 international river basins shared by two or more states, the legal frameworks governing transboundary watercourses have never been more critical. The 1997 UN Convention on the Law of the Non-Navigational Uses of International Watercourses (UNWC), which entered into force in 2014, represents the most comprehensive codification of customary international water law, though significant gaps and implementation challenges persist.

The UNWC enshrines two foundational and often competing principles: equitable and reasonable utilization (Article 5) and the obligation not to cause significant harm (Article 7). The tension between upstream development rights and downstream protection interests has generated substantial controversy, particularly in the Nile and Mekong river basins.

The Nile Basin presents a paradigmatic case. The 1959 Nile Waters Agreement between Egypt and Sudan, which allocated virtually the entire flow between the two states, was concluded without the participation of upstream riparians including Ethiopia and Uganda. Ethiopia's construction of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) has challenged this allocation regime, with Egypt invoking prior use and historical rights while Ethiopia asserts equitable entitlement as the source of over 85% of the Blue Nile's flow.

In the Mekong basin, the 1995 Mekong Agreement established the Mekong River Commission (MRC) as a basin-wide governance body. However, China and Myanmar, as upper riparians, are not full members. Chinese dam construction on the upper Lancang-Mekong has dramatically altered seasonal flow patterns, generating downstream impacts in Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam that raise serious questions under the no-harm principle.
author: Lamia Akhter

title: Universal Jurisdiction and the Prosecution of International Crimes
excerpt: An assessment of how national courts exercise universal jurisdiction over war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide, and the diplomatic friction this generates.
content:
Universal jurisdiction — the power of a national court to try individuals for crimes considered so grave that they threaten the international community as a whole, regardless of where the offense occurred or the nationality of the accused — stands as one of the most ambitious and controversial doctrines in contemporary international law.

The legal foundation for universal jurisdiction over the 'core crimes' of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and torture rests on a combination of treaty obligations and customary international law. The 1984 Convention Against Torture (CAT) was a pivotal instrument, obligating state parties to establish jurisdiction over torture regardless of nationality under the aut dedere aut judicare principle — prosecute or extradite.

The Pinochet case (1998-1999), in which the UK House of Lords held that former Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet could be extradited to Spain for acts of torture, marked a watershed moment. For the first time, a senior former head of state was denied immunity before a foreign court for serious human rights violations, signaling that the mantle of sovereignty could not indefinitely shield perpetrators of mass atrocities.

Belgium emerged as an early champion of expansive universal jurisdiction, passing legislation in 1993 and 1999 that permitted prosecution of international crimes with no connection to Belgium whatsoever. However, the ICJ's Arrest Warrant case (Congo v. Belgium, 2002) struck down the issuance of an international arrest warrant against a sitting Congolese foreign minister, ruling that serving government officials retain immunity ratione personae before foreign national courts.
author: Lamia Akhter

title: The Right to Life Under International Human Rights Law: Scope and Limitations
excerpt: A doctrinal analysis of Article 6 of the ICCPR and its interpretation by the Human Rights Committee, examining the extraterritorial application of the right to life in armed conflict.
content:
The right to life is the most fundamental of all human rights — the prerequisite for the enjoyment of all others. Enshrined in Article 3 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Article 6 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), it has generated an enormous body of treaty law, jurisprudence, and scholarly debate concerning its precise scope, its relationship with other bodies of law, and its application in extreme circumstances.

The Human Rights Committee's General Comment No. 36 (2019) represents the most authoritative contemporary interpretation of Article 6. The Comment clarifies that the right to life imposes three distinct obligations: the duty to refrain from arbitrary deprivation of life, the duty to protect individuals from third-party threats, and an expansive duty to take positive measures to address systemic threats including poverty, environmental degradation, and preventable disease.

Of particular scholarly interest is the extraterritorial application of Article 6 in situations of armed conflict. The traditional view held that international humanitarian law constituted the lex specialis displacing human rights law during active hostilities. However, the International Court of Justice's advisory opinion in the Nuclear Weapons case (1996) and its subsequent jurisprudence in the Wall advisory opinion (2004) and the DRC v. Uganda case (2005) established that human rights obligations continue to apply extraterritorially wherever a state exercises effective control.

This lex specialis debate has profound practical implications. Under IHL, incidental civilian casualties that are not excessive relative to military advantage may be lawful collateral damage. Under IHRL, every killing must be individually justified as necessary, proportionate, and non-arbitrary. The synthesis of these two frameworks remains deeply contested, with states generally preferring the more permissive IHL standard in military operations abroad.

The death penalty presents another critical dimension. While Article 6(2) of the ICCPR permits capital punishment in states that have not abolished it, provided certain procedural safeguards are met, the trend in international law is strongly abolitionist. The Second Optional Protocol to the ICCPR, with over 90 state parties, prohibits execution absolutely. The Human Rights Committee has increasingly interpreted Article 6 as moving toward prohibition of the death penalty as a matter of treaty obligation.
author: Lamia Akhter

title: The Geneva Conventions at 75: IHL Compliance in Modern Warfare
excerpt: Examining the enduring relevance and persistent violations of the four Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocols in contemporary armed conflicts in Gaza, Ukraine, and Sudan.
content:
The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their Additional Protocols of 1977 constitute the cornerstone of international humanitarian law — the body of rules that seek to limit the effects of armed conflict on persons and property. As the Conventions mark their 75th anniversary, their universal ratification (196 state parties) is matched only by the disturbing frequency of their violation in contemporary warfare.

Common Article 3, applicable to non-international armed conflicts, prohibits murder, torture, cruel treatment, and outrages upon personal dignity against persons taking no active part in hostilities. Yet the conflicts in Gaza, Sudan, and Myanmar have generated credible allegations of systematic violations including deliberate attacks on civilians, destruction of hospitals, starvation as a method of warfare, and the denial of humanitarian access.

The protection of medical personnel and facilities under the Geneva Conventions represents a particularly acute contemporary challenge. Article 19 of the Fourth Geneva Convention prohibits attacks on civilian hospitals, and the ICRC's customary IHL study (2005) identifies the protection of medical units as a norm binding on all parties. Despite this, the WHO's Surveillance System for Attacks on Healthcare (SSA) has documented thousands of attacks on health facilities in conflict zones since 2018.

The distinction principle — requiring parties to distinguish at all times between civilians and combatants, and between civilian objects and military objectives — is arguably the most fundamental rule of IHL. Its application in urban warfare against non-state armed groups that embed themselves within civilian populations poses profound interpretive challenges. The proportionality assessment under Additional Protocol I Article 51(5)(b), requiring that anticipated civilian harm not be excessive in relation to concrete and direct military advantage, has proven nearly impossible to enforce in practice.

The emergence of autonomous weapons systems raises urgent new IHL compliance questions. Meaningful human control over targeting decisions is arguably required by the rules of distinction, proportionality, and precaution. The ICRC has called for new legally binding rules on autonomous weapons, but state negotiations in the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) framework have stalled.
author: Lamia Akhter

title: UNCLOS and the South China Sea Arbitration: Maritime Law at a Crossroads
excerpt: An analysis of the landmark 2016 South China Sea arbitral award under UNCLOS Annex VII and China's rejection of the tribunal's jurisdiction — implications for the law of the sea.
content:
The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), often called the 'constitution of the oceans,' entered into force in 1994 after decades of negotiation. With 168 state parties, it is one of the most widely ratified international treaties. The Convention establishes a comprehensive regime governing maritime zones — from the 12-nautical-mile territorial sea to the 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone (EEZ) and the continental shelf — and provides for compulsory dispute settlement through the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), the ICJ, or Annex VII arbitral tribunals.

The 2016 Award in the South China Sea Arbitration (Philippines v. China) tested the limits of UNCLOS jurisdiction and China's compliance with the Convention's compulsory dispute settlement regime. The Annex VII tribunal, constituted under the Permanent Court of Arbitration, issued a landmark ruling on 12 July 2016 finding that China's historic rights claims within the 'nine-dash line' were incompatible with UNCLOS and had no legal basis. The tribunal further found that certain Chinese activities — including construction of artificial islands, interference with Philippine fishing vessels, and operation of maritime law enforcement vessels in Philippine EEZ waters — violated the Convention.

China rejected the tribunal's jurisdiction and refused to participate in proceedings, characterising the award as 'null and void.' This stance has generated profound questions about the enforceability of international arbitral awards and the limits of compulsory dispute settlement. While the Philippines has not actively sought enforcement of the award, it has been cited by ASEAN member states and third parties in diplomatic exchanges and legal submissions concerning South China Sea disputes.

The case also raised important questions about the legal status of low-tide elevations, rocks, and islands under UNCLOS Article 121. The tribunal's application of the Article 121(3) test — distinguishing 'rocks' (entitled only to territorial sea) from 'islands' (entitled to an EEZ and continental shelf) — based on the capacity to sustain human habitation or an economic life of their own has significant implications for disputed features throughout the world's oceans.

The South China Sea dispute underscores the tension between UNCLOS's ambitious dispute settlement framework and the political realities of major power compliance. Without a Security Council mechanism for enforcement, compliance with international arbitral awards ultimately depends on diplomatic pressure, reputational costs, and the long-term interests of states in maintaining a rules-based maritime order.
author: Lamia Akhter

title: The 1951 Refugee Convention: Protection Gaps and 21st-Century Challenges
excerpt: A critical assessment of the 1951 Refugee Convention's definition of 'refugee' and how climate displacement, persecution by non-state actors, and mass influx challenge its protective framework.
content:
The 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees and its 1967 Protocol constitute the cornerstone of the international refugee protection regime. The Convention's refugee definition — a person outside their country of nationality owing to a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group, or political opinion — has proven remarkably durable, yet increasingly contested as the nature of forced displacement has transformed over seven decades.

The most acute contemporary challenge is climate displacement. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) projects that climate change could displace between 200 million and 1 billion people by 2050. Yet climate-driven displacement falls squarely outside the 1951 Convention's definition: climate is not a recognised persecution ground, and the threat typically emanates from environmental conditions rather than state or non-state actor persecution. The 2020 decision of the UN Human Rights Committee in Teitiota v. New Zealand, while declining to find a violation on the facts, recognised that climate-related threats could in principle engage non-refoulement obligations — a significant doctrinal development, though of limited immediate practical effect.

Persecution by non-state actors presents a second major challenge. The Convention's drafters envisaged state persecution as the paradigmatic threat, and many national refugee determination systems have historically required a failure of state protection as an element of the refugee definition. However, in contexts such as gang violence in Central America, persecution by armed non-state groups in Syria and Somalia, and domestic violence, the source of persecution is private actors rather than the state.

The 'particular social group' ground has been progressively expanded by courts in various jurisdictions to cover women fleeing gender-based violence, LGBTQ+ individuals, and family members of dissidents. However, interpretation remains inconsistent across states, generating significant protection gaps.

The principle of non-refoulement — the prohibition on returning a person to a territory where they face serious risk of persecution — is widely recognised as a norm of customary international law, binding even on states not party to the Convention. However, its practical implementation is undermined by border externalisation policies, offshore processing arrangements, and pushback practices that prevent asylum seekers from reaching a state's territory and triggering its protection obligations.
author: Lamia Akhter

title: WTO Dispute Settlement Reform and the Appellate Body Crisis
excerpt: An examination of the US blockade of Appellate Body appointments since 2017, the resulting paralysis of WTO dispute settlement, and proposed reforms to restore a functioning appeals mechanism.
content:
The World Trade Organization's dispute settlement system, established by the Dispute Settlement Understanding (DSU) annexed to the WTO Agreement in 1994, was long regarded as the jewel in the crown of the multilateral trading system — a rules-based mechanism through which member states could resolve trade disputes through binding adjudication rather than economic coercion. The two-tier system, comprising panels at first instance and the seven-member Appellate Body on appeal, generated an extensive jurisprudence across goods, services, and intellectual property over more than two decades.

The system entered crisis in 2017 when the United States began blocking the appointment of new Appellate Body members, citing concerns about judicial overreach, the failure of the Appellate Body to comply with its 90-day review deadline, and alleged 'gap-filling' beyond what the DSU authorises. By December 2019, the Appellate Body fell below its quorum of three members, effectively suspending its operations. Since then, any appeal filed against a panel ruling disappears into a procedural void — parties can appeal 'into the void,' preventing a ruling from becoming legally operative.

The crisis has had profound practical consequences. Over 25 appeals have been filed into the void as of mid-2026, creating legal uncertainty about the status of panel rulings in cases involving agricultural subsidies, tariffs, and intellectual property. The European Union, China, Canada, and other members have established the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement (MPIA) under DSU Article 25 as a temporary workaround, but the United States and several other major traders are not parties.

Reform proposals have proliferated. The Walker Process, named after former New Zealand Ambassador David Walker, identified areas of convergence among members on Appellate Body reform relating to the 90-day deadline, precedent, advisory opinions, and the scope of review. However, fundamental disagreements remain about the degree to which the Appellate Body should be constrained to the text of WTO agreements and prohibited from interpretive creativity.

The dysfunction of WTO dispute settlement has accelerated the fragmentation of international trade governance, with major trading powers increasingly turning to bilateral and regional dispute settlement arrangements, Section 301 unilateral measures, and geopolitically motivated tariffs that circumvent multilateral disciplines.
author: Lamia Akhter

title: Sections 122A and 122B of the Transfer of Property Act 1882: Bangladesh's 2026 Amendment on Lifetime Usufruct and Heba
excerpt: Bangladesh's 2026 amendment to the Transfer of Property Act 1882 inserted Sections 122A and 122B, creating a statutory framework for gifts with lifetime usufruct retention. This article examines the corpus-usufruct split mechanism, the irrevocability regime under Section 122B, the classical Heba doctrine and the ayn-manafi distinction, and the savings clause that preserves Muslim personal law alongside the new statutory route.
content:
Across Bangladesh, a quiet crisis has been unfolding for decades. Elderly parents, trusting in filial duty, gift their homes and lands to their children only to find themselves dispossessed, evicted, or reduced to dependents in the very houses they built. The law offered no structured mechanism for a parent to transfer property while retaining the right to live in it, collect its rents, or enjoy its income for life.

In 2026, Bangladesh's Jatiya Sangsad enacted an amendment to the Transfer of Property Act 1882 (TPA) inserting **Sections 122A and 122B of the Transfer of Property Act 1882**, creating a statutory framework for gifts with lifetime usufruct retention. This is a Bangladeshi enactment. Both Bangladesh and India inherited the TPA 1882 from British colonial legislation, but the two countries have diverged substantially in their amendments. India has no equivalent provision.

Section 122A allows a donor to transfer the corpus of property to a donee while retaining enumerated usufruct rights for life. Section 122B governs irrevocability and the narrow grounds for revocation. Section 122A(4) contains a savings clause that expressly preserves Heba under Muslim personal law. The analysis that follows examines both provisions in statutory detail, assesses the classical Heba doctrine and the ayn-manafi distinction, and considers the practical implications for donors, donees, and practitioners.

## Legislative Context: Why Bangladesh Amended the Transfer of Property Act in 2026

The social mischief that prompted this amendment is neither obscure nor debatable. Elderly donors who transferred immovable property to their children had no legally enforceable right to continue occupying or deriving income from that property. The existing TPA framework treated a completed gift as an absolute transfer. Once possession passed, the donor was a stranger to the property unless a contractual arrangement had been separately executed, and even then, enforcement was uncertain.

Bangladesh's legislative trajectory with the TPA has been independent since 1971. The 2026 amendment is the most significant reform to the gift provisions. India addressed elderly vulnerability through the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, which empowers tribunals to cancel transfers but creates no usufruct retention mechanism. That statute is remedial, not structural.

The parliamentary process was contentious. Opposition came principally from Hefazat-e-Islam and Jamaat-e-Islami, both fearing that the amendment could circumvent Islamic inheritance rules (faraiz) by enabling parents to distribute property to favoured heirs during their lifetime, bypassing Quranic distribution ratios. The government maintained that the amendment created an optional, secular mechanism and did not touch personal law. This tension between codified statute and uncodified personal law runs through the entire analysis.

Indian practitioners encountering clients with Bangladesh property must understand that no equivalent statutory route exists in India. The closest Indian mechanism is the life-interest clause drafted into a gift deed, a contractual arrangement without a statutorily defined usufruct right or its own revocation regime.

## Section 122A Explained: Gift with Lifetime Usufruct Retention

Section 122A of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 limits its application to specified relationships: parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, and spouses. The legislature targeted the relationships where donor vulnerability is greatest and betrayal of trust most acute. A parent who gifts property to a child and is then denied access suffers a harm qualitatively different from a commercial donor-donee dispute. By restricting eligibility, the legislature avoided creating a general statutory usufruct regime that could complicate commercial transactions.

The mechanism operates through a corpus-usufruct split. The corpus (ownership and title) transfers to the donee immediately upon registration of the gift deed. The donor retains enumerated usufruct rights: the right to occupy the property, to collect rents from tenants, and to receive income generated by the property. The usufruct is a real right, not merely a personal licence. It attaches to the property and binds successors in title. This distinction matters enormously. A personal licence can be revoked; a real right runs with the land.

Registration is mandatory under the Registration Act. The gift deed must be registered at the Sub-Registrar's office with both parties present or duly authorized. This stands in deliberate contrast to Heba under Muslim personal law, which requires no registration and no writing. The formality requirement under Section 122A serves an evidentiary purpose: it creates an unambiguous, publicly recorded instrument defining the donor's retained rights with specificity.

The provision addresses the risk of the donee predeceasing the donor. If the donee dies before the donor, the donee's heirs inherit the corpus, but the donor's usufruct survives. Without this protection, the donee's heirs, who may be strangers or hostile to the donor, could extinguish the usufruct. The statute forecloses this possibility.

Automatic extinguishment operates on the donor's death. The usufruct terminates without further formalities. Full ownership consolidates in the donee or the donee's heirs. No further deed, court order, or additional registration is required.

Sub-section (4) is pivotal. It reads: "This section does not restrict or affect ordinary gifts, hiba under Muslim law or any other legally recognised method of property transfer." Section 122A creates a parallel statutory route for gifts with usufruct retention. It does not replace, restrict, or modify existing transfer mechanisms, including Heba. A Muslim donor in Bangladesh may choose either route. The two coexist.

## Section 122B Explained: Irrevocability, Revocation Grounds, and Judicial Oversight

The default rule under Section 122B is irrevocability. A registered gift under Section 122A cannot be revoked unilaterally by the donor. This is stated independently of Section 126 TPA, which governs the general revocability of gifts and permits revocation where the gift deed itself contains a revocation condition. Section 122B is a self-contained regime.

The first exception permits revocation by mutual consent. Both donor and donee must agree, and their agreement must be embodied in a registered deed specifying the ground of genuine necessity: financial hardship, medical need, familial crisis, or educational requirement. The legislature required not just agreement but documented justification, presumably to prevent coerced revocations.

The second exception permits judicial intervention where the donee's consent genuinely cannot be obtained. This covers incapacity, disappearance, or unreasonable refusal. The court must be independently satisfied that genuine necessity exists and that the donee's consent genuinely could not be obtained. This is not a rubber-stamp jurisdiction; the court exercises a substantive evaluative function.

Section 126 TPA allows a gift to contain a revocation condition, and the donor may revoke by exercising that reserved right. Section 122B is narrower: it does not permit the donor to reserve a unilateral right of revocation in the gift deed itself.

Under Hanafi Muslim personal law, Heba is generally revocable before delivery of possession (qabza). After delivery, revocability is limited by several bars, including the donor-donee relationship (gifts to close relatives within prohibited degrees become irrevocable on delivery). Section 122B is stricter than Heba post-registration: once the Section 122A gift is registered, revocation requires either mutual consent with documented genuine necessity or a court order. No unilateral revocation is possible.

## Heba Under Muslim Personal Law: Classical Doctrine and the Ayn-Manafi Distinction

In both India and Bangladesh, Heba is governed by Muslim personal law, not the TPA. In India, Section 129 TPA expressly excludes gifts made by Muslims from Chapter VII. Section 2 TPA contains a broader savings clause preserving rules of Mohammedan law inconsistent with TPA provisions. In Bangladesh, the same principle applies.

The three essentials of a valid Heba are well settled. First, Ijab: a declaration by the donor of intention to gift. Second, Qabul: acceptance by the donee. Third, Qabza: delivery of possession. No registration or writing is required. As Mulla states in the Principles of Mahomedan Law, Section 138, Heba is "a transfer of property, made immediately and without any exchange." This informality is a defining characteristic that distinguishes Heba from the formality-heavy regime of Section 122A.

The ayn-manafi distinction is the critical doctrinal key to understanding the relationship between Heba and Section 122A. Muslim jurisprudence strictly distinguishes between the corpus (ayn) and its usufruct (manafi). Over the corpus, only absolute dominion is recognized: heritable and unrestricted in time. Any condition attached to a gift of the corpus inconsistent with absolute dominion is rejected as repugnant. But interests limited in time can be created in the usufruct.

The foundational authority is the Privy Council dictum: "Over the corpus of property the law recognises only absolute dominion, heritable and unrestricted in point of time; and where a gift of the corpus seeks to impose a condition inconsistent with such absolute dominion the condition is rejected as repugnant; but interests limited in point of time can be created in the usufruct of the property and the dominion over the corpus takes effect subject to any such limited interests."

A Hiba that transfers the corpus unconditionally while the donor retains the usufruct for life is valid under Muslim law. The condition operates on the manafi, not the ayn. The donee receives absolute dominion over the corpus; the donor's retained interest is limited to the usufruct and limited in time to the donor's lifetime. The Supreme Court of India, in Dharmrao Sharanappa Shabadi v. Syeda Arifa Parveen (2025), reaffirmed: "Possession is the soul of a valid Hiba."

## Heba, Heba-bil-Iwaz, and Heba-ba-Shart-ul-Iwaz: Distinctions and Interaction with the 2026 Amendment

Heba in its simple form is a gratuitous transfer requiring Ijab, Qabul, and Qabza, with no consideration. Under Hanafi law, it is revocable before delivery of possession, subject to exceptions where the donor and donee are within prohibited degrees of relationship. After delivery, revocability is limited.

Heba-bil-Iwaz is a gift with immediate exchange. The donee immediately pays iwaz (consideration) to the donor. Once paid, the transaction acquires the character of a sale and becomes irrevocable. Registration is required because the transaction is essentially a sale. The leading authority is Khajooroonissa v. Roushan Jehan, which established that Heba-bil-Iwaz, once completed by payment of iwaz, is treated as a sale for all legal purposes.

Heba-ba-Shart-ul-Iwaz is a gift with a stipulation for future return. The donor makes the gift with a condition that the donee will pay iwaz at some future date. The gift is revocable until the iwaz is actually paid. Once paid, it becomes irrevocable and is treated as a sale.

| Type | Consideration | Revocability | Registration | Character |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Heba | None | Revocable before delivery | Not required | Pure gift |
| Heba-bil-Iwaz | Immediate | Irrevocable once iwaz paid | Required | Sale character |
| Heba-ba-Shart-ul-Iwaz | Stipulated future | Revocable until iwaz paid | Required once complete | Sale character once complete |

Section 122A(4)'s savings clause means none of these forms is displaced by the amendment. For simple Heba, the Section 122A usufruct retention structure mirrors what Muslim law already permits under the ayn-manafi doctrine: the corpus transfers to the donee, the usufruct is retained by the donor. The statutory route codifies this structure with registration and formality. For Heba-bil-Iwaz and Heba-ba-Shart-ul-Iwaz, both involve consideration and shade into sale rather than gift. Practitioners advising clients on these compound instruments should not conflate them with the Section 122A regime.

## Does Section 122A Affect Heba? Savings Clause, Structural Alignment, and the Religious Controversy

The apparent conflict between Sections 122A and 122B of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 and Heba is largely illusory. This is the finding that close analysis reveals, and that the religious-political controversy has obscured.

On its face, Section 122A allows a donor to gift property while retaining usufruct. This might appear to conflict with Heba's requirement of unconditional transfer and qabza. If the donor retains the usufruct, has the donor truly delivered possession? These questions are reasonable but ultimately misplaced.

The conflict is illusory for three reasons. First, the savings clause. Section 122A(4) expressly states that the section "does not restrict or affect ordinary gifts, hiba under Muslim law or any other legally recognised method of property transfer." Muslims choose between the statutory route and traditional Heba. Section 122A is elective, not mandatory.

Second, structural alignment with the ayn-manafi doctrine. Section 122A's corpus-transfers-but-usufruct-retained structure is exactly what Muslim law already permits under the Privy Council rule. The statutory structure does not innovate on the substance of what is permissible. It codifies an existing legal possibility with formality and registration.

Third, optionality. Section 122A creates an additional option. It imposes nothing on any donor, Muslim or non-Muslim.

The religious-political controversy, however, is real and consequential even if the legal conflict is not. Hefazat-e-Islam and Jamaat-e-Islami objected that a parent could use Section 122A to give property to a favoured child, bypassing the Quranic 2:1 inheritance ratio, while retaining usufruct for life. The counter-argument: this same circumvention is possible through ordinary gift, sale, or traditional Heba. Section 122A does not create a new mischief; it codifies an existing option with more documentary formality.

The Bangladesh Law Minister addressed this during the 2026 parliamentary debate: "The reform does not touch inheritance law at all. The statute explicitly maintains that traditional hiba and existing personal laws remain fully operational."

Section 122A is a complementary provision, not a competing one. For non-Muslim donors, it provides statutory clarity previously achievable only through imprecise life-interest drafting. For Muslim donors, it adds an optional, registered, irrevocable alternative without displacing a single rule of Heba.

## Practical Implications: Drafting, Registration, Banking Complications, and Post-Death Procedures

Draft the gift deed under Section 122A with precision. Specify four elements: (1) the property, described with particularity sufficient to identify the corpus; (2) the usufruct rights retained, enumerated specifically (occupation, rents, income, or any combination); (3) the relationship between donor and donee, confirming statutory eligibility; and (4) an express acknowledgment that the gift is made under Section 122A TPA. Omitting any element risks challenge to validity.

Register the deed at the Sub-Registrar's office. Both parties must attend or provide duly executed powers of attorney. Stamp duty implications are uncertain. Confirm with the relevant revenue authority whether usufruct retention affects valuation for stamp duty purposes. Expect stamp duty to be assessed on the full value of the corpus, not the discounted value of ownership subject to usufruct, though this remains to be settled.

Banking complications are significant and underappreciated. The donee holds title, but the donor holds the usufruct. A mortgagee cannot obtain vacant possession on default during the donor's lifetime. The usufruct binds successors in title, reducing collateral value significantly. Lenders will be cautious about accepting mortgages on Section 122A properties. Ensure mutation records reflect the split: donee as owner, donor as usufructuary.

Post-donor-death procedure is simple. The usufruct extinguishes automatically. The donee or donee's heirs apply for mutation to remove the usufruct notation, updating the record to reflect unencumbered ownership. If the donee predeceases the donor, a succession certificate or probate may be needed to establish the heirs' title to the corpus.

Indian practitioners: this framework does not exist in India. Do not assume Indian TPA provisions apply to property situated in Bangladesh.



## Key Case Law: Heba, Usufruct, and Property Transfers

### Abdul Fata Mahomed Ishak v. Russomoy Dhur Chowdhry (1894) 22 IA 76 (Privy Council)

This is the foundational authority for the ayn-manafi distinction in Muslim property law. The Privy Council held that while absolute dominion over the corpus must be unrestricted in time, interests limited in duration can validly be created over the usufruct. The principle directly validates the legal structure of Section 122A: the donee receives the corpus, and the donor retains only a lifetime usufruct — a manafi interest, not an ayn interest. Any condition purporting to restrict absolute dominion over the corpus itself would be void as repugnant; a condition operating only on the usufruct is valid.

### Khajooroonissa v. Roushan Jehan (1876) 2 Cal 184 (Privy Council)

The Privy Council held that a Heba-bil-Iwaz — a gift accompanied by an immediate exchange of consideration — acquires the character of a sale once the iwaz is paid. It becomes irrevocable and requires registration as a sale would. This case distinguishes Heba-bil-Iwaz from simple Heba (which requires no writing or registration) and from Section 122A gifts (which require registration but involve no consideration). Practitioners must not conflate these three distinct instruments.

### Nawazish Ali Khan v. Ali Raza Khan AIR 1948 PC 134 (Privy Council)

The Privy Council examined the extent to which conditions may be attached to Muslim gifts. It reaffirmed that conditions repugnant to the absolute nature of the transfer of the corpus are void, but confirmed that the law does not prohibit arrangements by which only the usufruct is transferred or retained for a limited period. This case supports the position that a donor retaining a lifetime usufruct while transferring the corpus does not render the gift void under Muslim personal law.

### Mst. Hussenabi v. Husensab Hasan Sajanwala AIR 1961 SC 1330 (Supreme Court of India)

The Supreme Court of India held that delivery of possession (qabza) is an essential requirement for a valid Heba. A Heba without actual or constructive delivery is incomplete and revocable. This case is directly relevant to Section 122A: under the statutory route, registration substitutes for the informality of Heba, and the donor's retained usufruct constitutes a structured form of continued possession — not a defect in delivery, but a recognised real right. The distinction between the statutory registered route and the personal law Heba route is most clearly illustrated by contrasting the qabza requirement with Section 122A's registration requirement.

### S. Vanitha v. Deputy Commissioner, Bengaluru Urban District (2020) 15 SCC 1 (Supreme Court of India)

The Supreme Court upheld the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, which permits tribunals to void transfers made by elderly parents to children who subsequently fail to maintain them. The Court held that such transfers, though completed, can be set aside in the interests of elderly welfare. This decision reflects the legislative concern that prompted Bangladesh's 2026 amendment. Where India adopted a remedial post-transfer cancellation mechanism, Bangladesh's Section 122A takes a structural preventive approach: the donor never fully surrenders the property, retaining a real usufruct right enforceable during their lifetime without needing tribunal intervention.

### Dharmrao Sharanappa Shabadi v. Syeda Arifa Parveen (2025) (Supreme Court of India)

The Supreme Court reaffirmed that possession is the soul of a valid Hiba. The Court held that a purported Hiba without delivery of possession remains revocable and does not confer title on the donee. This 2025 ruling reinforces why the Section 122A statutory route offers a critical advantage for donors who wish to retain possession: rather than creating ambiguity about whether qabza has occurred, Section 122A explicitly recognises the donor's continued possession as a statutory usufruct right, not as an impediment to the transfer of the corpus.

## Frequently Asked Questions on Sections 122A and 122B TPA 1882

### Does Section 122A of the TPA apply in India?

No. Section 122A was enacted by Bangladesh's Jatiya Sangsad in 2026. India has no equivalent provision.

### Can a Muslim donor in Bangladesh use Section 122A instead of Heba?

Yes. Section 122A(4) preserves Heba. A Muslim donor may choose either route. The statutory route offers registration, documentary certainty, and a defined revocation regime. Traditional Heba offers informality and compliance with religious obligation.

### Is a gift under Section 122A revocable?

Irrevocable by default under Section 122B. Revocation is permitted only by mutual consent documented in a registered deed specifying genuine necessity, or by judicial intervention where the donee's consent genuinely cannot be obtained.

### What happens if the donee dies before the donor?

The donee's heirs inherit the corpus. The donor's usufruct rights survive and continue until the donor's death. The donor cannot be dispossessed by the donee's heirs.

### Does Section 122A override Islamic inheritance (faraiz) rules?

No. Section 122A governs inter vivos gifts, not testamentary succession. Property transferred by gift leaves the donor's estate during their lifetime and is not subject to faraiz distribution on death. This is no different from traditional Heba.

### What is the difference between Section 122A and Section 126 TPA?

Section 126 governs general revocability and permits revocation where the gift deed contains an express revocation condition. Section 122B is stricter: it does not permit the donor to reserve a unilateral right of revocation. Revocation requires mutual consent with genuine necessity or a court order.

title: The Paris Agreement and Loss & Damage: A New Frontier in Environmental Law
excerpt: An analysis of the Santiago Network and the COP28 Loss and Damage Fund — examining whether international environmental law is developing meaningful liability for climate harm.
content:
The Paris Agreement, adopted in December 2015 and entering into force in November 2016, marked a paradigm shift in international climate governance. Departing from the top-down, binding emissions targets of the Kyoto Protocol, Paris adopted a bottom-up architecture of nationally determined contributions (NDCs) paired with a transparency and global stocktake mechanism designed to ratchet ambition over time. The Agreement's temperature targets — limiting warming to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C — have become reference points for climate litigation, policy, and scientific assessment worldwide.

The inclusion of loss and damage in Article 8 of the Paris Agreement represented a hard-won victory for small island developing states and least developed countries, which have contributed least to cumulative greenhouse gas emissions yet face disproportionate climate impacts. However, the COP21 decision accompanying the Agreement explicitly stated that Article 8 'does not involve or provide a basis for any liability or compensation' — a compromise that secured US participation but fundamentally limited the provision's legal force.

COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh (2022) achieved a historic breakthrough with the agreement to establish a dedicated loss and damage fund, operationalised at COP28 in Dubai (2023). The Fund — hosted by the World Bank on an interim basis — received initial pledges of approximately $700 million, a fraction of the estimated $400 billion annual loss and damage that developing countries are projected to suffer by 2030. The governance arrangements, including who can access the fund, the definition of loss and damage, and the relationship between the fund and existing climate finance mechanisms, remain deeply contested.

Parallel developments in climate litigation are reshaping the legal landscape. The ICJ's advisory opinion on states' obligations regarding climate change — requested by the UN General Assembly at Vanuatu's initiative and expected in 2024-2025 — may clarify the content of international law obligations under the UNFCCC, the Paris Agreement, customary law, and human rights law. Domestic courts have issued landmark rulings holding governments liable for inadequate climate action in the Netherlands (Urgenda), Germany (constitutional court), and Pakistan (Lahore High Court).

The tension between the Paris Agreement's facilitative architecture and the urgent need for enforceable climate obligations reflects a deeper challenge in international environmental law: the difficulty of generating binding, enforceable obligations on issues where state interests — particularly those of major fossil fuel producers — diverge sharply from the collective interest in climate stability.

title: Remedies for Constitutional Crisis: A Comparative Guide to Restoring the Rule of Law
excerpt: Most constitutional crises do not arrive with tanks in the streets. They arrive with legislation, judicial appointments, and procedural maneuvers. This comparative guide examines judicial, legislative, electoral, constitutional design, and civil society remedies across India, South Korea, Brazil, Poland, Hungary, and Israel — and explains why no single remedy suffices.
author: Lamia Akhter

title: Arbitration and English Commercial Law: A Student's Guide to the 2025 Reforms and Beyond
excerpt: England hosts roughly 5,000 arbitrations per year, contributing an estimated GBP 2.5 billion to the national economy. The Arbitration Act 2025, which came into force on 1 August 2025, is the most significant reform in three decades. This guide covers the statutory framework, separability, Kompetenz-Kompetenz, Section 69 appeals, the AA 2025 reforms, confidentiality, enforcement, and London's global competitive position.
author: Lamia Akhter

title: Alternative Dispute Resolution in Common Law Countries: A Legislative Review
excerpt: The Centre for Effective Dispute Resolution reported a 92% mediation settlement rate in England and Wales. Between Churchill v Merthyr Tydfil [2023], the CPR 2024 amendments, and the Arbitration Act 2025, common law systems have shifted from encouraging ADR to mandating it. This legislative review traces that evolution and examines the tensions between compulsion, access to justice, and norm development.
author: Lamia Akhter

title: Can a Country Carry the Death Penalty Against a Foreign National? How Saudi Arabia Weaponizes Its Legal System Against Migrant Workers
excerpt: In October 2026, Saudi Arabia executed two Bangladeshi nationals in Mecca. Their embassy found out from the news. This article examines how Saudi Arabia systematically violates VCCR Article 36, CAT Article 15, and Arab Charter Article 6 in capital cases involving migrant workers — and why the international legal system has largely failed to stop it.
author: Lamia Akhter

title: Declaring Bankruptcy in Bangladesh: Can You Get Debt Relief?
excerpt: The Bankruptcy Act 1997 provides a statutory pathway to discharge, but in 26 years only 533–638 petitions have ever been filed. This article examines the legal framework, the Artha Rin Adalat conflict, corporate insolvency under the Companies Act 1994, and the proposed Insolvency and Bankruptcy Ordinance 2025.
author: Lamia Akhter
content:
# Is It Possible to Get Relief from Debt by Declaring Bankruptcy in Bangladesh?

In twenty-six years since the **Bankruptcy Act 1997** took effect, Bangladesh has seen only 533 to 638 bankruptcy petitions filed across the entire country. Between 2016 and 2020, courts disposed of exactly two cases out of eleven filed. The statute does provide a pathway to debt discharge, and this article walks through every relevant provision. But the near-total dormancy of this system forces a harder question: can a debtor in Bangladesh actually obtain meaningful relief through bankruptcy? The statutory framework, case data, the unresolved conflict with Artha Rin Adalat proceedings, and the proposed Insolvency and Bankruptcy Ordinance 2025 all reveal an answer far more complicated than the statute suggests.

## The Short Answer: Statutory Relief Exists but Remains Practically Elusive

Yes, the [Bankruptcy Act 1997](https://bdlaws.minlaw.gov.bd/act-869.html) provides for adjudication of bankruptcy and eventual discharge. A debtor whose debts exceed Tk. 20,000 can file a voluntary petition under Section 13. Creditors holding at least Tk. 5,00,000 in unsecured debt can file after a debtor commits an **act of bankruptcy** under Section 9, most commonly by failing to satisfy a statutory demand within 90 days.

Upon adjudication, Section 31 vests all of the bankrupt's property in the **Official Receiver** automatically. The court imposes a moratorium. Section 47 then provides the mechanism for **discharge**, which can be absolute or conditional.

Discharge is extraordinarily rare in practice. The case of Apurna-Zahid Fashion Limited, filed in August 2000, was still pending as of 2021. Over twenty years without resolution. Sections 44 and 48 impose a 50% recovery threshold as one ground for refusing discharge. The debtors most desperately in need of a fresh start are the least likely to obtain one.

The system also operates on a critical structural divide. The Bankruptcy Act 1997 governs individuals and partnerships. Corporate insolvency falls under the Companies Act 1994 winding-up provisions. These are entirely separate regimes with different courts, different procedures, and different outcomes.

## Statutory Framework Under the Bankruptcy Act 1997

Section 9 defines the **acts of bankruptcy** that trigger creditor petitions: absconding to avoid debts, making a fraudulent transfer of property, giving written notice of inability to pay, or suffering execution against property. The most common trigger is a debtor's failure to comply with a creditor's statutory demand for Tk. 5,00,000 or more within 90 days.

A debtor can also self-petition under Section 13, with a much lower threshold of Tk. 20,000 in debt. The petition goes to the **District Court** sitting as the Bankruptcy Court. After examination, the court issues an **Order of Adjudication**, published in the official Gazette.

Section 32 exempts certain property from the bankruptcy estate: tools of trade, household necessities, and a homestead of up to 2,500 square feet in urban areas. The total exemption is capped at Tk. 3,00,000. Legislators have never adjusted this cap for inflation since 1997, and in real terms the exemption has eroded dramatically. Practitioners advising debtors should read this alongside the broader framework of immovable property rights under Bangladesh law — the [intersection of property transfer rules and insolvency exemptions](/articles/sections-122a-122b-tpa-1882-bangladesh-2026-lifetime-usufruct-heba) raises important questions about how heba and usufruct interests survive adjudication.

Section 47 governs **discharge**. The court may grant absolute or conditional discharge after considering the bankrupt's conduct and the creditors' recovery. Section 51 carves out **non-dischargeable debts**: government debts, debts arising from fraud "to which [the bankrupt] was a party," and maintenance orders.

Section 28 allows defendants in bankruptcy suits to apply for dismissal on grounds including solvency. The Appellate Division confirmed in *Emdadul Haque Bhuivan v. Bankruptcy Court*, 8 BLT (AD)-175 that a guarantor cannot obtain dismissal under Section 28(b) simply by virtue of their guarantor status. They must affirmatively prove capacity to repay and that they are not a willful defaulter.

Section 94 imposes severe restrictions on an **undischarged bankrupt**: no bank loans, disqualification from Parliament, the judiciary, and public office. These restrictions persist indefinitely until the court grants discharge.

Section 60 provides a **claw-back period** of 15 years. Courts can reverse any transfers made within this window. The United Kingdom applies a two-year look-back; India's IBC 2016 also uses two years. Bangladesh's 15-year provision deters voluntary filing.

Section 43 offers an alternative through a **composition or scheme of arrangement**. This requires approval by creditors holding two-thirds of the total debt value, plus court sanction. A successful composition can annul the adjudication order entirely, but this provision sees minimal use in practice. The composition mechanism is essentially an in-court form of alternative dispute resolution — for comparative context on how common-law jurisdictions are modernising out-of-court settlement frameworks, see the [legislative review of ADR in common-law countries](/articles/adr-common-law-countries-legislative-review).

## Why the System Barely Functions: Practical Barriers to Bankruptcy Relief

The numbers tell the story. Only 533 to 638 total bankruptcy petitions were filed in the 26 years since the Act took effect. Between 2016 and 2020, eleven cases were filed. Two were disposed of. Approximately Tk. 2,600 crore remains stuck in pending cases. As of June 2023, 172 cases were still under trial, with banks claiming Tk. 4.24 billion.

Banks avoid the system entirely. Bangladesh Bank spokesperson Md Mezbaul Haque stated plainly: "The banks are not considering going to the bankruptcy courts in good numbers to file the cases as they deem it as not viable or effective option to recover the default loan." Barrister Khan Mohammad Shamim Aziz put it more bluntly: "Banks always lose in bankruptcy suits in the sense that they cannot recover default loans."

From the debtor's side, the incentives are equally discouraging. The 50% recovery threshold under Sections 44 and 48 means a deeply insolvent debtor, one who cannot pay half of what is owed, faces denial of discharge. The Tk. 3,00,000 exemption cap set in 1997 has not been revised despite decades of inflation. The 15-year claw-back under Section 60 exposes virtually every significant transaction a debtor has ever made.

Bangladesh's **non-performing loan** ratio reached 36% by September 2025, with Tk. 6.44 lakh crore in distressed bank debt. Total distressed assets climbed to approximately Tk. 11 lakh crore by early 2026, roughly 60% of banking sector loans. Yet the bankruptcy system resolves virtually nothing. Only one corporate bankruptcy was declared in the last decade.

## The Artha Rin Adalat Conflict and the Strategic Defaulter Loophole

Bangladesh operates a dual-track system for debt resolution that creates a dangerous gap. The **Artha Rin Adalat Act 2003** governs loan recovery by banks and financial institutions through specialized **Money Loan Courts**. The Bankruptcy Act 1997 governs collective insolvency proceedings. No statutory coordination mechanism exists between the two.

Banks overwhelmingly prefer the Artha Rin Adalat. Section 12 of that Act permits out-of-court enforcement against secured property. Section 34 authorizes civil imprisonment for up to six months. Section 42 requires a 75% appeal deposit, discouraging challenges. These are aggressive creditor tools.

Research published on ResearchGate analyzing the effort to rescue Bangladesh's Bankruptcy Act 1997 found a critical loophole: if a debtor files a bankruptcy petition while Artha Rin Adalat proceedings are pending, the Artha Rin Adalat suit automatically becomes invalid. Courts have not authoritatively resolved which regime prevails when the two collide. This gap is exploitable.

The High Court Division addressed the boundary between the two regimes in *Shamshad Asif v. Additional District Judge*, HCD, 52 DLR 138 (1999). Al-Baraka Bank had obtained Artha Rin Adalat decrees against the petitioner and simultaneously filed bankruptcy proceedings. The court held that bankruptcy suits proceed independently of decree proceedings; the nature and issues of each forum differ fundamentally. Crucially, the court confirmed that res judicata does not bar a bankruptcy petition simply because an Artha Rin Adalat decree already exists against the same debtor. The two regimes serve different purposes and neither forecloses the other.

The Artha Rin framework has its own enforcement vulnerabilities. In *Dr. Kazi Sirazul Islam v. Artha Rin Adalat No. 1, Dhaka*, HCD, 2022(1) LNJ 263 (2023), the court addressed Section 12(3) of the Artha Rin Adalat Act 2003, which conditions subsequent suit-filing on a prior failed auction attempt. A mortgagor had obtained a stay, frustrated the auction, and then argued the bank had "failed" to sell within the statutory meaning. The court rejected this. Obstruction engineered by the mortgagor through a meritless writ petition cannot satisfy the statutory "failure" requirement. Banks may restart enforcement once such stays are vacated.

The practical result is devastating. Large **strategic defaulters**, responsible for much of the Tk. 6.44 lakh crore NPL crisis, face neither effective recovery proceedings through the Artha Rin Adalat nor meaningful insolvency consequences through the Bankruptcy Act. They occupy a zone of impunity between two broken systems.

For practitioners advising bank creditors, forum selection must account for the invalidation risk. A borrower's voluntary bankruptcy petition can frustrate bank recovery proceedings, but it triggers automatic vesting of all assets in the Official Receiver under Section 31.

## Corporate Insolvency: The Companies Act 1994 Winding-Up Path

The Bankruptcy Act 1997 does not apply to corporations. It covers individuals and partnerships only. Corporate insolvency is governed exclusively by **Part IX of the Companies Act 1994** (Sections 234 through 308), which provides for winding-up proceedings before the High Court Division sitting as the **Companies Bench**.

Section 241 establishes the primary ground relevant here: inability to pay debts. A creditor petition triggers the appointment of an **Official Liquidator**, who realizes the company's assets and distributes proceeds according to statutory priority.

In practice, this regime is almost entirely unused for insolvency purposes. Only one corporate winding-up on insolvency grounds has been declared in the last decade. The process is slow, expensive, and offers no rescue mechanism.

Bangladesh has no equivalent to India's **Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process** under the IBC 2016, with its time-bound 180-day resolution period (extendable by 90 days). There is no equivalent to the United States' **Chapter 11** reorganization. There is no debtor-in-possession financing framework. Section 46 of the Bankruptcy Act, which theoretically provides for reorganization of non-individual debtors, has been described as a "dead letter" in LegalSeba's analysis. It has never been successfully used.

Bangladesh has also not adopted the [UNCITRAL Model Law on Cross-Border Insolvency](https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/insolvency/modellaw/cross-border_insolvency). Foreign creditors have no statutory framework for participation, and assets held abroad fall outside the reach of domestic proceedings.

## The Proposed Insolvency and Bankruptcy Ordinance 2025: Reform on the Horizon

A draft **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Ordinance 2025** has been prepared under the interim government with involvement from BAIRA (Bangladesh Association of Insolvency Restructuring and Administration). As of October 2026, it has not been enacted as operative law. The Chambers Banking Regulation 2026 guide references a proposed "Insolvency and Bankruptcy Act 2026," suggesting possible enactment under a revised title.

The draft Ordinance represents a paradigm shift. Its primary objective is **going-concern rescue**, moving away from the current liquidation-first approach. Creditor value optimization is positioned as a secondary objective. The proposals include cross-border insolvency provisions, accelerated reorganization procedures, a dedicated **Insolvency Tribunal**, and a regulatory body analogous to India's **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI)**.

The reform agenda draws directly on the framework principles the [World Bank has long advocated for effective insolvency systems](https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/financialsector/brief/insolvency-and-debt-resolution) — predictability, creditor value maximization, and going-concern preservation. Bangladesh's proposed Ordinance tracks these principles, though implementation capacity remains the central obstacle. For practitioners familiar with how England's Arbitration Act 2025 modernised a similarly stagnant statutory regime, the [parallel reform experience in English commercial dispute resolution](/articles/arbitration-english-commercial-law-2025-reforms-guide) offers a useful comparative lens on what legislative modernisation can and cannot achieve without institutional change.

A separate but related development: the **Bank Resolution Ordinance 2025** was enacted in May 2025 and granted Bangladesh Bank authority to intervene in failing banks. This led to the forced merger of five Islamic banks into Sammilito Islami Bank PLC in September 2025. That ordinance addresses systemic banking resolution, not general insolvency for individual or corporate debtors.

The direct driver of reform is the NPL crisis. With a 36% non-performing loan ratio and total distressed assets approaching Tk. 11 lakh crore by early 2026, the status quo is untenable. Significant implementation uncertainties remain. Bangladesh has no trained cadre of insolvency professionals, political transition risks cloud the legislative timeline, and the banking sector may resist a framework that forces collective proceedings over bilateral recovery.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the minimum debt threshold to file a bankruptcy petition in Bangladesh?

It depends on who files. A creditor must hold at least Tk. 5,00,000 in unsecured debt and demonstrate an act of bankruptcy under Section 9 of the Bankruptcy Act 1997, most commonly by issuing a statutory demand that goes unsatisfied for 90 days. A debtor can file a voluntary petition under Section 13 with debts as low as Tk. 20,000.

### Can a company declare bankruptcy under the Bankruptcy Act 1997?

No. The Bankruptcy Act 1997 applies only to individuals and partnerships. Corporate insolvency is governed by Part IX of the Companies Act 1994 (Sections 234 through 308), which provides for winding-up proceedings before the High Court Division. No corporate rescue or reorganization mechanism equivalent to India's IBC or US Chapter 11 currently exists.

### How long does the bankruptcy process take in Bangladesh?

No statutory time limit applies. In practice, cases routinely take 10 to 20 years or more. The Apurna-Zahid Fashion Limited case was filed in August 2000 and remained pending as of 2021. Between 2016 and 2020, only 2 out of 11 filed cases were disposed of. The system offers no meaningful timeline for resolution.

### What property is exempt from the bankruptcy estate?

Section 32 of the Bankruptcy Act 1997 exempts tools of trade, personal effects, household necessities, and a homestead of up to 2,500 square feet in urban areas. The total value of exempt property is capped at Tk. 3,00,000. This cap has not been revised since 1997, making it severely inadequate in current economic conditions.

### Will the proposed 2025 Ordinance change the bankruptcy system?

If enacted, the draft Insolvency and Bankruptcy Ordinance 2025 would introduce time-bound resolution, a dedicated Insolvency Tribunal, corporate rescue procedures, a fresh-start provision, and cross-border insolvency mechanisms. As of October 2026, the Ordinance remains in draft form and has not been enacted into law. Implementation will depend on political will and institutional capacity building.
